# Scoped Values

Scoped values pass context down a call chain without adding a parameter to every
intermediate method. This example binds an immutable request ID for a service
call, reads it in a repository method, and observes nested bindings being
restored automatically. A correct `ThreadLocal` comparison shows the
improvement: **the scoped-value API enforces the binding’s lifetime**, including
restoration when an operation throws. Scoped values became final in Java 25
through [JEP 506: Scoped Values](https://openjdk.org/jeps/506); no preview flags
are required for this example.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- bind a request ID for the dynamic scope of a call and retrieve it in a
  downstream method without passing it through intermediate parameters;
- explain nested rebinding and restoration on normal and exceptional completion;
- compare the explicit save, restore, and removal required by a `ThreadLocal`
  with the binding lifetime enforced by the scoped-value API;
- distinguish an unbound key from a bound value and describe what `get()` does
  outside a binding; and
- explain the limits of scoped values: implicit dependencies, per-thread
  bindings, and no automatic thread safety for mutable objects.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)
JDK or newer. Ensure `JAVA_HOME`, `java`, and `javac` select that JDK.

## The program to inspect

### The requirement — temporary request context

Consider a service that calls a repository through intermediate methods. An
explicit `requestId` parameter is straightforward, but each intermediate method
must forward it even if only the repository needs it.

The context must remain available throughout the service call. Nested work needs
a temporary request ID, after which the outer ID must be restored. Both normal
and exceptional completion must leave the context as it was before the call.
Once the outer request finishes, its ID must not remain for the next request
handled by the same thread.

### ThreadLocal — the programmer manages the lifetime

A `ThreadLocal` can meet this requirement correctly. The comparison below uses
non-null request IDs and reserves `null` to mean “no request context”. It uses a
plain `ThreadLocal` with its default `null` initial value; this is a helper for
this request-context convention, not a general-purpose helper for arbitrary
thread-local values.

Before replacing the current ID, save it. In `finally`, restore that ID if there
was an outer context, or remove the value if this was the outermost call. The
`finally` block handles normal return and exceptions alike.

```java
private static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>();

static void runWith(final String requestId, final Runnable action) {
    final String previous = REQUEST_ID.get();
    REQUEST_ID.set(requestId);
    try {
        action.run();
    } finally {
        if (previous == null) {
            REQUEST_ID.remove();
        } else {
            REQUEST_ID.set(previous);
        }
    }
}
```

Simply calling `remove()` in every `finally` block would lose the outer request
ID when nested work finishes. Omitting cleanup would retain the replacement ID.
**Saving the previous value, restoring it, and removing the outermost value are
responsibilities of this application code.** These are consequences of the
[`ThreadLocal` API contract](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/ThreadLocal.html).

### ScopedValue — the API enforces the lifetime

The corresponding scoped-value code expresses the same lifetime directly:

```java
private static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance();

static void runWith(final String requestId, final Runnable action) {
    ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, requestId).run(action);
}
```

**Both versions can produce the correct result. With scoped values, the API
guarantees restoration; the programmer does not implement it in `finally`.**
Returning or throwing ends the nested binding and reveals the enclosing one.
Ending the outermost binding leaves the key unbound. This is the
[`Carrier.run` contract](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/ScopedValue.Carrier.html#run(java.lang.Runnable)).

| Lifetime responsibility    | Correct `ThreadLocal` baseline            | `ScopedValue`                                    |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Preserve the outer context | Save the previous value before `set`      | Enclosing binding remains intact                 |
| End a nested override      | Restore the saved value in `finally`      | Nested binding ends automatically                |
| Handle an exception        | Execute the same restoration in `finally` | Binding ends automatically; exception propagates |
| End the outermost request  | Call `remove()` in `finally`              | Key becomes unbound automatically                |

The runnable program uses scoped values. The `ThreadLocal` snippet above is the
comparison baseline for understanding the lifetime work that disappears.

`RequestContext` owns a private `ScopedValue<String>` key. The static key is
shared; its bindings are per-thread. `runWith` creates a mapping with `where`
and establishes the binding while `run` executes its action synchronously in the
calling thread. Creating the mapping alone does not bind anything.

The **dynamic scope** includes methods called directly or indirectly by that
action. `requestId()` retrieves the innermost binding. With no binding, `get()`
throws `NoSuchElementException`; `isBound()` allows an explicit check.
Completion of the action, including exceptional completion, restores the
previous binding. No manual removal or cleanup block is needed.

```java
package demo;

final class RequestContext {

    private static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance();

    private RequestContext() {}

    static void runWith(final String requestId, final Runnable action) {
        ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, requestId).run(action);
    }

    static String requestId() {
        return REQUEST_ID.get();
    }

    static boolean isBound() {
        return REQUEST_ID.isBound();
    }
}
```

### Reading, rebinding, and restoring

`Main` binds `request-42` and calls `service`, which calls `repository` without
forwarding the request ID. The repository retrieves it through `RequestContext`.
A nested call temporarily binds `nested-request`. A second nested call binds
`failing-request` and deliberately throws an exception. Both calls restore
`request-42` before the service resumes; the exception still propagates to its
catch block. When the outer call returns, the key is unbound again.

Follow each return to its caller: `service` performs no save, restore, or
removal. The single `ScopedValue.where(...).run(...)` call in `RequestContext`
establishes the lifetime for all these cases.

Rebinding creates a nested scope; it does not mutate the enclosing binding. The
bound object here is an immutable `String`. Binding an object does not freeze
that object or make its mutable fields thread-safe.

```java
package demo;

public class Main {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Before request: bound=" + RequestContext.isBound());
        RequestContext.runWith("request-42", Main::service);
        System.out.println("After request: bound=" + RequestContext.isBound());
    }

    private static void service() {
        repository("Service entry");

        RequestContext.runWith("nested-request", () -> repository("Nested scope"));
        repository("After nested scope");

        try {
            RequestContext.runWith("failing-request", () -> {
                repository("Failing scope");
                throw new IllegalStateException("demonstration failure");
            });
        } catch (final IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        repository("After failing scope");
    }

    private static void repository(final String stage) {
        System.out.println(stage + ": requestId=" + RequestContext.requestId());
    }
}
```

The execution trace is deterministic because every call runs sequentially in the
main thread. Scoped-value binding and restoration follow the API contract. There
is no cross-thread publication or happens-before claim in this example, and
scoped values provide no mutual exclusion for mutable shared state.

A new thread created with `Thread.start` or a thread builder does not inherit
these bindings automatically. The API supports inheritance through
`StructuredTaskScope`, which is a separate preview API in Java 25 and is outside
this lesson. Do not assume that submitting work to an executor carries the
caller’s scoped-value context.

Prefer explicit parameters when they keep dependencies clear. Scoped values suit
one-way transmission of unchanging context down a call chain; they are not a
general replacement for mutable per-thread state or return values. Keep the key
private and expose only the operations callers need.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from `examples/scoped-values`. Choose one of these two
execution paths; both produce the same trace.

1. Compile and run using the Maven `exec` plugin.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

   The request ID follows the innermost active binding.

   ```
   ...
   Before request: bound=false
   Service entry: requestId=request-42
   Nested scope: requestId=nested-request
   After nested scope: requestId=request-42
   Failing scope: requestId=failing-request
   Caught: demonstration failure
   After failing scope: requestId=request-42
   After request: bound=false
   ...
   ```

2. Build and test the application, then run its modular JAR.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   ```shell
   java \
     --module-path './target/libs' \
     --module demo
   ```

   The same binding lifecycle, without Maven output.

   ```
   Before request: bound=false
   Service entry: requestId=request-42
   Nested scope: requestId=nested-request
   After nested scope: requestId=request-42
   Failing scope: requestId=failing-request
   Caught: demonstration failure
   After failing scope: requestId=request-42
   After request: bound=false
   ```

In either trace, `Before request` and `After request` report `bound=false`.
`Nested scope` reads `nested-request`, and `Failing scope` reads
`failing-request`. Both `After nested scope` and `After failing scope` read
`request-42`. These are scope-lifetime observations, not timing measurements.

Read the trace as evidence of the lifetime contract:

| Trace point           | Observed context | Work required in the `ThreadLocal` baseline                    |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `After nested scope`  | `request-42`     | Restore the saved outer ID in `finally`                        |
| `After failing scope` | `request-42`     | Restore the saved outer ID in `finally`, despite the exception |
| `After request`       | `bound=false`    | Remove the outermost request ID in `finally`                   |

A correct `ThreadLocal` implementation can deliver the same request-context
lifecycle. The improvement demonstrated here is that **binding restoration is
guaranteed by the scoped-value API**, so the application has no manual
restoration or removal logic to get wrong. This is not a performance comparison.

The tests run by `./mvnw clean package` also check that an unbound lookup
throws, that exceptions propagate unchanged, that an outer failure leaves
the key unbound, and that sequential requests do not retain each other’s
binding.
